transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mrs. Al-Rashid, thank you for coming in today. I need to talk with you about your immunotherapy dose from Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is everything alright? I felt a bit tired after the infusion, but I thought that was normal.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have something difficult to tell you. We made a mistake. Your medication was given on the wrong day of your treatment cycle because of a calendar error on my part.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The wrong day? But I came when I was told. Did I do something wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, you did everything perfectly. This was my error. I am so sorry that this happened. I take full responsibility for this mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not understand. If it was the wrong day, does that mean the medicine is not working? Does it mean the cancer is coming back?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is completely understandable that you feel scared right now. Hearing that a mistake was made in your cancer treatment is terrifying. I can see how shocking this is for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I trust the doctors. I always do what the doctors say. I just want to be healthy for my grandchildren. I did not expect this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know how much your family means to you, and the fact that you’ve been so diligent and trusting makes it even more upsetting that I let this happen. I am deeply sorry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But what does this mean for the cycle? Is the dose ruined?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: In the pharmaceutical cycle, the timing is meant to be precise to maximize the effect. Because we gave it a few days early, there is a possibility that this specific dose was less effective than it should have been.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Less effective. So it was a waste?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is not a total waste, but it wasn't the optimal timing.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel very confused. I thought the schedule was fixed. How could a calendar be wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I entered the date incorrectly into the system. It was a human error on my end.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I cannot believe this. I just want to know if I am safe.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are safe. The dose itself was correct and there is no danger of an overdose or a toxic reaction.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But I feel like I have lost time. We are fighting this disease and now we have lost a week.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can hear the frustration and the worry in your voice. It feels like a setback when you are fighting so hard to get well.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not know what to say. I have never had a doctor tell me they made a mistake like this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is a lot to take in. Let me just check, do you understand why the timing was important and what happened with the calendar?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, you put the wrong date and the medicine might not work as well this time.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct. Now, I want to tell you exactly how we are going to fix this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How can you fix a day that has already passed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We cannot change Tuesday, but we can adjust the rest of your cycle. I have already consulted with the oncology pharmacist and the attending physician. We are going to shift your next three appointments by exactly four days to get you back on the correct rhythm.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So everything moves?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. Your next dose, which was supposed to be next Monday, will now be on Friday. I will personally send you a revised calendar by this evening, and I will call you tomorrow morning to make sure you received it and that the new dates work for your transport.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I will have to tell my son to change his schedule.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that is an extra burden on your family. To make sure this never happens again, I have updated our clinic's double-check protocol. From now on, two different nurses must verify the cycle date against the original chart before any immunotherapy is administered.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose that is good. I just feel very unsettled.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely understand. It is very distressing to lose that sense of certainty in your care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to make sure this is the only mistake.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have reviewed your entire file, and every other dose and lab test has been exactly on track. This was an isolated error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is there anything I should watch for?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, there are no new side effects to worry about. Just continue with your usual medications.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think I need to go home and talk to my family.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. I have to go now as I have a clinic, but I will get that email to you quickly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are rushing me now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry, I just want to make sure you get home to your family. Let's wrap this up and I will call you tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I still feel very shaken.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know. Just remember that the plan is set and we are moving forward. I will talk to you tomorrow morning.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language at the end of the encounter ('I have to go now', 'Let's wrap this up') after the patient expresses feeling shaken.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, and comprehension was checked once ('do you understand why the timing was important...').

A.justification: The resident used direct apology language, took full personal responsibility ('This was my error'), and maintained accountability throughout.

R.justification: The resident named specific emotions ('scared', 'terrifying', 'frustration', 'worry') and referenced the patient's specific mention of her grandchildren.

T.justification: The resident provided specific next steps with timelines (revised calendar tonight, call tomorrow), a patient role (checking transport), and a prevention plan (double-check protocol).
